transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-20 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lucas Ramirez (Head of Platform, Thunderbolt AI), Priya Singh (SRE), Owen Park (CTO)

Summary:
Thunderbolt AI is evaluating Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private for a low-latency real-time recommendation service used in multiplayer games. Primary concerns: reserved GPU sizing, tenant isolation, burst-to-4x traffic patterns during events, latency SLOs (95p < 80ms), encryption/KMS (Azure Key Vault), SOC 2 compliance, and on-prem path as contingency. They asked about failover playbooks, warm pools/prewarm behavior, and pricing for reserved nodes + burst credits.

Topics:
- Workload profile and burst patterns
- Isolation and tenancy model (hot pools, tenant fencing)
- Failover and fallback to hosted model
- Prewarm / warm pool strategies and costs
- Compliance: SOC 2, encryption at rest/in transit, KMS integration
- Timeline and procurement constraints

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros—I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood side, and with me is Ravi, our SE focused on Dedicated and Private deployments.
[00:12] Lucas: Hey Maya, hey Ravi. Lucas here, Head of Platform at Thunderbolt AI. Thanks for making time.
[00:18] Priya: Priya, SRE. We'll likely be the ones running the fist fights when things go sideways.
[00:22] Owen: Owen, CTO. I'll listen in; happy to answer higher-level questions.
[00:26] Maya: Awesome. Goal for today is to understand your peak patterns and isolation needs so we can recommend reserve sizing and failover options. Roughly 45 minutes, leave some time for next steps. Sound good?
[00:34] Lucas: Sounds good. We'll jump in.
[00:35] Ravi: Quick note—if it helps later I can pull up the docs for prewarming and our warm-pool cost model.

[02:05] Lucas: To give context: we run a real-time recommendation engine for a live multiplayer title. Typical traffic is low steady-state, then during tournaments/events traffic spikes 3-4x for short bursts (10-40 minutes). We need 95th percentile inference latency under 80ms for player-facing calls.
[02:25] Priya: Most requests are short sequences, 32 tokens or under, but throughput is high. We also can't have noisy neighbors; when one tenant runs training or batch jobs, it breaks our tail latency.
[03:02] Maya: Got it. Sounds like isolation and tail latency are the big ones. Have you considered Dedicated pools vs Hosted fallback model?
[03:12] Lucas: We like the economics of hosted for baseline, but we need guaranteed performance for peaks. Thinking about a dedicated reserved pool (or a warm reserved hot pool) for critical traffic and fallback to hosted API for non-critical flows.
[03:29] Ravi: That's a common pattern—dedicated for SLO-critical traffic, hosted for overflow. We support routing policies that prefer dedicated, with automatic fallback to hosted variants when capacity is exhausted. We also support model variants (quantized or smaller models) as fallbacks.

[04:10] Priya: A couple of concrete questions: how fast can you spin up burst capacity? And how does warm pool prewarm behave—do you keep GPUs hot and is there a prewarm cost?
[04:22] Ravi: Prewarm: you can configure a warm-pool size that maintains kernels and KV states warmed. There's a continuous cost for reserved warm nodes; it's cheaper than full-on spare nodes because they can be smaller or quantized for faster resume. We also offer burst credits for short bursts if you have reserved capacity. For spin-up to fully ready, warm pool to fully warmed serving path is typically under 90s; cold spin from zero can be several minutes depending on model size.
[04:51] Lucas: Ninety seconds is ok but sometimes our spikes are sudden—tournament queue opens and we get hit instantly. Can we do instant failover to hosted and still maintain the same model?
[05:04] Maya: You can. We allow routing to point to hosted model variants with compatible behavior. There will be slight differences if the hosted variant is quantized differently; we can test parity with your eval prompts.

[06:10] Owen: Security: we need KMS integration (we're on Azure Key Vault), SOC 2 Type II, SSO via Okta, and audit logs for every inference. How does Redwood handle that?
[06:24] Ravi: For Dedicated we support customer-managed keys via our KMS integrations; Azure Key Vault is supported. We can enable envelope encryption so keys never leave your control. SOC 2 artifacts and the compliance pack can be shared—I'll add them to the follow-up. Audit logs and per-route tracing are available; you can ship logs to your SIEM or retain in Redwood console.
[06:46] Priya: Do the audit logs include per-token traces or just request-level metadata? We need enough detail to debug tail cases.
[06:54] Ravi: Currently request headers, request/response sizes, latency breakdowns and model selection events are logged. Full token-level traces can be enabled in debug mode but with cost and privacy considerations; we usually advise redacting PII.

[08:12] Lucas: Another operational question—how do you enforce tenancy isolation? We want burst traffic from other tenants, or internal batch jobs from our non-prod tenant, to never impact prod.
[08:26] Ravi: Dedicated Reserved can be configured with soft or hard isolation. Hard isolation pins GPUs to your tenancy (no multi-tenancy). Soft isolation uses fenced hot pools where compute is dedicated but control plane can borrow under emergency. For strict SLAs you want hard isolation. Our hot-pool topology supports tenant fencing at node-level.
[08:50] Priya: What's the blast radius if a hardware failure occurs on a pinned node? Do you prewarm standby nodes or have automatic failover?
[08:58] Ravi: For pinned nodes we recommend N+1 standbys. There is an automated failover into standby nodes, but warm standby reduces time to recovery. If you want near-zero impact you can provision hot-standbys that are warmed and ready. That increases cost, but it's the usual trade-off.

[10:12] Lucas: Cost is a big factor—our finance team will push back on always-on hot standbys. We need guidance on sizing so we don't overcommit.
[10:21] Maya: We can do a sizing exercise. If you share typical QPS and token distribution we can model reserved node counts and warm-pool sizing. We also provide a cost/latency tradeoff sheet.
[10:33] Owen: Quick procurement note—we have a 60-day procurement cycle and prefer 12-month committed pricing for reserved capacity. Do you offer monthly vs annual commits?
[10:44] Maya: Yes, reserved commitments can be monthly or annual; annual has better pricing. We'll include both options in the pricing matrix.

[12:15] Priya: What's the difference between Dedicated and Private here? If we need on-prem later, how big a lift is migrating?
[12:26] Ravi: Private is essentially running Redwood control plane in your VPC or on-prem package. The APIs are consistent but Private brings additional network and install controls. Migration is straightforward if you keep model versions and config consistent, but there is an integration cost: networking, KMS, and potential hardware procurement. We have reference on-prem manifests and a runbook.
[12:50] Lucas: For now we're leaning Dedicated but want Private as a contingency in case regulations tighten.
[12:59] Maya: That's a common path—start on Dedicated, then move to Private if needed.

[14:05] Lucas: One more technical—how does the runtime handle KV cache across sequence continuity? We rely heavily on KV cache for context, and eviction can harm latency.
[14:18] Ravi: We manage KV cache per-session and have configurable cache retention policies. For Dedicated we can tune cache sizes and prioritize your tenant's KV allocations to reduce cache churn. There was a minor note in our docs where KV cache got transcribed as 'KV cash' sometimes in automated notes—sorry for the typo in the docs.
[14:34] Priya: Ha, yes I saw that.

[15:44] Lucas: For burst modeling—our peak bursts historically last 15-30 minutes. We might see a 3.5x spike for the first 10 minutes then taper. If we reserve nodes for average peak it's wasteful. Are there hybrid models—like partial reserved + burst credits?
[15:58] Ravi: Yes, hybrid is typical: reserve a baseline of capacity to cover median peaks and then have either warm-pool sizing to cover the initial spike and fallback to hosted for overflow, or reserve a small hot standbys pool plus burst credits. We can also suggest model quantization and smaller model variants to absorb overflow with less cost.
[16:30] Lucas: Can you run a simulated burst with our sample load so we can see tail latency behavior?
[16:40] Maya: Absolutely. If you can share a representative load generator and a small prompt corpus, we can run a hosted simulation or spin up a small Dedicated trial environment.

[18:10] Priya: Networking—we need VPC peering and strict egress controls. Does Redwood Dedicated allow VPC peering?
[18:19] Ravi: Yes, Dedicated supports VPC peering and private networking. For Private deployments you'd have full control. For Dedicated hosted in our cloud region we offer VPC peering and restricted egress with customer NAT. We'll share network diagrams.

[19:45] Owen: I want to call out parity of model behavior—if we route to hosted fallback, we must guarantee minimal semantic drift. How do you evaluate that?
[19:59] Ravi: We recommend running an eval suite—sample prompts, quality checks, and A/B comparisons. Redwood Optimize has a regression alerting feature tied to prompt sets; we can run the same tests across variants and give a delta report.

[22:05] Lucas: Are there any hard limitations on model size for warm pools? We use a 30B model currently, but might move to 70B for specific tournament features.
[22:18] Ravi: Warm pools can handle larger models but cost and warm time grow. For 70B the warm-to-ready time is longer and you may need more reserved memory. Another option is a mixed fleet: keep a smaller 30B tuned variant warmed for the common path and enable a slower 70B path only for high-value calls.

[24:30] Priya: How do you price reserved nodes vs warm pool instances? Is warm pool cheaper because of shared memory or is it just a smaller instance type?
[24:44] Maya: Warm pool pricing is typically lower than fully warmed serving nodes because they can be configured to be smaller or use quantized flavors. But the pricing varies by region and GPU type. We'll include detailed per-GPU SKU pricing in the follow-up.

[26:05] Lucas: Any vendor lock-in concerns? If we wanted to move off after a year, how easy is it?
[26:15] Ravi: We provide model and config exports; the runtime uses standard model formats. Network and infra teardown is the main work. We also support pinned model versions and recommend a data egress plan in the contract.

[28:30] Priya: Regarding SLOs—what's Redwood's SLA for Dedicated? We need specifics for uptime and p95 latency commitments.
[28:40] Maya: Dedicated SLA covers uptime of the control plane and your reserved capacity. For latency SLOs we provide guidance and per-route SLO monitoring; contractual latency SLOs are available on enterprise contracts with accepted guardrails. We'll include template SLA language.

[30:05] Lucas: Competitors—someone internally suggested DeepServe because they have pre-baked gaming optimizations. How do you compare?
[30:14] Maya: DeepServe is focused on model-side optimizations for gaming but we differentiate on unified routing, observability, and enterprise controls. We'll share a competitive brief.

[32:20] Owen: On the timeline—if we decide to move forward, what is a realistic ramp for Reserved dedicated capacity?
[32:31] Ravi: From contract to live varies; typically 4-8 weeks including network setup, model onboarding, and warm-pool tuning. If you want quicker ramp we can do a hybrid start on Hosted then flip routes once Dedicated is ready.

[34:10] Lucas: Let's cover a couple of edge cases: sudden peak plus regional outage—can you failover across regions?
[34:21] Ravi: Yes—cross-region routing and automated fallback policies exist. However, model parity and cold-start times differ. We can replicate model artifacts to a standby region; that's an added cost.

[36:00] Priya: For the technical deep dive, Priya will need details on kernel selection, quantization tradeoffs, and batching behavior at short sequences. Who should lead that?
[36:12] Maya: Ravi can lead the deep dive. He'll walk through batching heuristics, kernel choices, and KV cache tuning.

[38:05] Lucas: Can you include an initial sizing sketch in the follow-up? Even rough numbers help our procurement.
[38:14] Maya: Yes—we'll model multiple scenarios: conservative, balanced, and aggressive (covering 4x short bursts).

[40:20] Owen: We should also consider a canary strategy for rollout. We prefer canary -> phased -> full. Does Redwood Console support canary and A/B routing?
[40:32] Ravi: Yes, canary rollouts, weighted traffic routing, and automatic fallback policies are supported. You can set thresholds to auto-rollback on regression alerts.

[42:05] Lucas: Priya—anything we missed from an SRE perspective?
[42:11] Priya: Just two things: our compliance team will likely ask for network flow logs and KMS proofs; and we want a runbook for incident scenarios involving warm pool exhaustion.
[42:23] Ravi: We'll include a runbook template and network flow guidance in the follow-up.

[45:00] Maya: Ok, quick recap and next steps: we'll send pricing and reserve options, KMS/SOC2 artifacts, schedule the technical 60-min deep dive with Priya and Lucas, and run a hosted burst simulation if you can share the load generator.
[45:17] Lucas: Sounds good. We'll share a load generator and sample prompts by EOB tomorrow.
[45:24] Maya: Great—we'll aim to have materials to you by Friday.

[46:50] Owen: One more thought—if we choose annual commit, is there any enterprise discount for multi-year?
[46:59] Maya: Yes, multi-year discounts are part of enterprise negotiations; we'll flag that to the sales ops team.

[48:30] Priya: Small nit: will test harnesses be able to collect p99 traces? We want to see tail behavior; p95 isn't enough for major tournaments.
[48:41] Ravi: You can enable extended tracing in test mode, but it has overhead. For p99 we usually advise dedicated profiling runs with a small set of traced sessions.

[50:05] Lucas: Ok, I think that's everything for now. Thanks all.
[50:12] Maya: Thank you, we'll follow up with docs and pricing.
[50:20] Owen: Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
